explain.say: The Moon makes no light of its own. The Sun always lights up half of it, and as the Moon orbits Earth each month, we see different amounts of that lit half.

faq.q: Why can't we see the new moon?
faq.a: At new moon, the Moon lies roughly between Earth and the Sun. The side facing us is unlit, and the Moon is lost in the Sun's glare, so we can't see it.
asks: Where is the Moon at new moon?

faq.q: Why is it called a quarter moon when it looks half full?
faq.a: Because the Moon has completed a quarter of its orbit since new moon. We see half of the face that points at us lit, which is a quarter of the Moon's whole surface.
asks: What is a first quarter moon?

faq.q: Why is the full moon so bright?
faq.a: At full moon we see the whole sunlit side face-on, and sunlight bounces straight back towards us. A full moon is about ten times brighter than a half moon.
asks: Why does the full moon light up the night?

faq.q: How long does a full cycle of phases take?
faq.a: About 29.5 days, from one new moon to the next. Our word month comes from moon, because early calendars were based on this cycle.
asks: How long is a lunar month?

faq.q: Are the Moon's phases caused by Earth's shadow?
faq.a: No, that is a common mix-up. Phases come from how much of the Moon's sunlit half we can see. Earth's shadow only falls on the Moon during a lunar eclipse.
asks: Does the Earth's shadow cause the phases of the Moon?

facts: A full cycle of lunar phases, from new moon to new moon, takes about 29.5 days.
The Moon is lit by sunlight; it makes no light of its own.
Seen from the southern hemisphere, the Moon's phases look flipped left to right compared with the northern hemisphere.
